posts.title: Best cheap standing desk (and the spec that decides whether it wobbles)
posts.summary: Lift mechanism, weight capacity and the wobble test: choosing a budget sit-stand desk that is actually usable.
intro: Budget standing desks fail at the same point: they wobble at standing height. A desk that shakes while you type gets lowered once and never raised again.
The variables that decide it are the frame type, the capacity rating and the width — not the number of memory presets.

shortlist.title: Two-leg electric sit-stand desk, 120 cm
shortlist.who: A single monitor, a laptop and a keyboard, in a room with a standard-width space.
shortlist.choose_if: you want electric height adjustment at the lowest sensible price and can keep the load light.

shortlist.title: Four-leg or T-frame desk, heavier duty
shortlist.who: People with two monitors, or anyone who has already returned a wobbly desk.
shortlist.choose_if: you want noticeably less movement at standing height and can spend more and wait for stock.

shortlist.title: Manual crank sit-stand desk
shortlist.tag: Best if you rarely change height
shortlist.who: People who will set a height once and leave it.
shortlist.choose_if: you want the lowest price and the fewest parts to fail, and do not mind winding it.

table: Matching a top to your own space

skip.what: Judging a desk by its weight capacity alone
skip.why: Capacity tells you what it will lift, not how stable it is when raised. A desk rated for 80 kg can still wobble under a 6 kg monitor because the frame is thin.

skip.what: A very wide top on a two-leg frame
skip.why: Wobble scales with width and height. Beyond roughly 140 cm, a two-leg frame starts to feel unstable at standing height — that is when a T-frame or four legs is the answer.

skip.what: Paying extra for app control and many presets
skip.why: Two presets (sit and stand) is all anyone uses. The premium goes into electronics rather than the frame, which is where the money needs to be.

decide: Measure your seated and standing elbow heights, then check the desk's height range covers both.
One monitor? Two-leg is usually fine.
Two monitors or an existing wobble complaint? Go T-frame or four-leg.
Never change height? A manual crank saves money and has less to break.
posts.outro: Assemble on a hard floor, not carpet — a wobbly desk on carpet is often just an uneven base. Retighten the frame bolts after the first week of use.

posts.title: Best dehumidifier for a basement (and how to size it properly)
posts.summary: Pint capacity, temperature range and drainage: sizing a dehumidifier for a basement rather than guessing.
intro: Dehumidifiers are sold by pint capacity per day, and buying the wrong size is the most common mistake in both directions: too small never dries the space, too large cycles constantly and wastes power.
Basements add two extra constraints: they are colder than the rest of the house, and they usually have a drain you can use instead of emptying a tank.

shortlist.title: 30-pint dehumidifier with continuous drain
shortlist.who: Damp basements up to roughly 60 m² with a floor drain or a sink nearby.
shortlist.choose_if: you want to set it and forget it, with a hose rather than a tank.

shortlist.title: 20-pint dehumidifier, compact
shortlist.tag: Best for small or mildly damp spaces
shortlist.who: Cellars, crawl spaces and small basements with light damp.
shortlist.choose_if: the space is small and you do not want a large unit taking up floor.

shortlist.title: 50-pint dehumidifier
shortlist.who: Basements with visible damp, a history of flooding, or laundry drying indoors.
shortlist.choose_if: you have a real moisture problem and the space is large.

skip.what: Sizing a cold basement using a warm-room rule of thumb
skip.why: Most refrigerant dehumidifiers lose efficiency sharply below about 15°C and can frost up. A cold basement may need a desiccant type instead — check the operating temperature range before buying, not after.

skip.what: A unit with no continuous drain option
skip.why: In a basement you will be emptying a tank every day in a wet spell, and the first time you forget, the tank overflows. A hose to a drain is the difference between a dehumidifier you keep and one you abandon.

skip.what: Buying the largest unit 'to be safe'
skip.why: An oversized unit short-cycles, which removes less water overall than a correctly sized one running steadily, and uses more electricity doing it.

decide: Measure floor area and note the temperature range of the basement.
Below about 15°C most of the time? Look at desiccant models rather than refrigerant.
Is there a floor drain or sink? If yes, buy a unit with a continuous drain hose.
Light damp up to ~60 m²? 30-pint is the sensible default.
posts.outro: A dehumidifier treats the symptom. If the basement has a persistent damp smell or efflorescence on the walls, the cause is usually drainage or waterproofing outside, and no dehumidifier fixes that.

posts.title: Best electric kettle for tea (and the temperature feature worth having)
posts.summary: Variable temperature, spout shape and capacity: choosing a kettle for tea rather than for speed.
intro: If you drink black tea and want it fast, almost any kettle works. If you drink green, white or oolong tea, water temperature is the whole game — boiling water scalds them and turns them bitter.
So the decision is really: do you need variable temperature, and how precise does it need to be?

shortlist.title: Variable-temperature kettle with selectable presets
shortlist.who: Anyone brewing green, white or oolong tea regularly.
shortlist.choose_if: you want repeatable temperatures without watching a thermometer.

shortlist.title: Gooseneck variable-temperature kettle
shortlist.tag: Best for pour-over coffee and delicate tea
shortlist.who: People pouring slowly and precisely, usually for pour-over coffee.
shortlist.choose_if: you want a controlled, narrow pour as well as temperature control.

shortlist.title: Basic fast-boil kettle
shortlist.who: Black tea, instant coffee, and anything that wants boiling water.
shortlist.choose_if: you only ever need boiling water and want to spend very little.

skip.what: A variable-temperature kettle with poor hold time
skip.why: If it drops back to room temperature in ten minutes, you will re-boil constantly. Check the keep-warm duration rather than the number of preset buttons.

skip.what: A plastic-bodied kettle for frequent tea
skip.why: Plastic can retain flavours, particularly if you also boil water for other uses. Glass or stainless steel is the safer long-term choice.

skip.what: Paying for temperature control when you only drink black tea
skip.why: Black tea wants water at or near boiling. You would be paying for a feature you never use.

decide: Only boiling water? Basic kettle — save the money.
Green, white or oolong tea? Variable temperature is genuinely worth it.
Pour-over coffee too? Gooseneck with variable temperature.
Check capacity against how many cups you make in one go — 1.7 L is the common default.
posts.outro: Temperature is the most useful variable in tea brewing, ahead of brand and ahead of brewing vessel. A cheap variable kettle beats an expensive fixed one for anything but black tea.

posts.title: Best budget monitor for working from home (and what to ignore)
posts.summary: Resolution, panel type and stand adjustability: what actually matters in a budget work monitor.
intro: For desk work — documents, spreadsheets, video calls — the spec sheet fights you. Contrast ratios and response times are marketed for gaming and matter far less than text clarity and a stand you can actually adjust.
The two things worth spending on are resolution and a height-adjustable stand. Everything else is secondary.

shortlist.title: 24-inch 1920x1200 IPS monitor
shortlist.who: People working with text, spreadsheets and multiple windows all day.
shortlist.choose_if: you want the extra vertical height that 1200 gives over 1080 without going to a much larger screen.

shortlist.title: 27-inch 2560x1440 IPS monitor
shortlist.tag: Best if you want more space
shortlist.who: People running two windows side by side without a second screen.
shortlist.choose_if: you have the desk depth for a 27-inch panel and want a sharper, larger canvas.

shortlist.title: Ultrawide 34-inch
shortlist.who: People who currently run two screens and dislike the bezel in the middle.
shortlist.choose_if: you want one continuous surface and have the width for it.

skip.what: A gaming monitor for desk work
skip.why: High refresh rate and low response time make no difference to documents, and the money comes out of panel quality and stand adjustment — the two things that do matter here.
The curve only helps at large widths where the edges would otherwise be far from your eye. On a 24 or 27-inch screen it usually just makes straight lines look slightly bowed.

skip.what: A monitor with a fixed tilt-only stand
skip.why: Almost every complaint about neck strain traces back to a screen that cannot be raised. If the stand is not height-adjustable, budget for a VESA arm as well.

decide: Measure your eye height when seated, then check the stand's height range reaches it.
Text-heavy work? Prefer higher resolution and IPS, not refresh rate.
Two windows side by side? 27-inch 1440p or an ultrawide.
Stand only tilts? Add a VESA arm to the budget before you buy.
posts.outro: A second-hand business monitor is often the best value in this category — offices sell off height-adjustable IPS panels constantly, and they usually have better stands than new budget models.

posts.title: Best refurbished laptop for students (and the two specs that matter)
posts.summary: Business-laptop refurbs, RAM and battery health: how to buy a used laptop that lasts a degree.
intro: A refurbished ex-business laptop is usually the best value in student computing: sturdy chassis, replaceable parts, and a fraction of the price of a new consumer machine.
The trap is buying on price and ignoring two things that decide whether it lasts: the amount of RAM and the condition of the battery.

shortlist.title: Ex-business 14-inch, 16 GB RAM, upgraded SSD
shortlist.who: Students running a browser, documents and a video call at the same time.
shortlist.choose_if: you want a machine that will stay usable for the length of a course without being fragile.

shortlist.title: Ex-business 13-inch ultraportable
shortlist.who: Students who carry a laptop to every class and care about weight.
shortlist.choose_if: you want something light and are willing to accept a smaller screen for it.

shortlist.title: Refurbished 2-in-1 convertible
shortlist.who: Students who write or annotate by hand in lectures.
shortlist.choose_if: you want a pen-capable screen and can accept fewer ports and harder repairs.

skip.what: 8 GB RAM in a machine you expect to last three years
skip.why: It is the first thing to become a bottleneck, and on many thin laptops it is soldered and unupgradable. 16 GB is the difference between a laptop that lasts the course and one you replace halfway.

skip.what: Any refurb without a stated battery health figure
skip.why: A worn battery is the hidden cost that wipes out the saving. Ask for the cycle count or a battery health percentage; if the seller will not provide it, treat the battery as needing replacement.

skip.what: Buying the cheapest listing from an unknown seller
skip.why: On ex-business machines, the difference between listings is usually whether the keyboard, screen and hinges have been checked. Seller rating and a stated returns policy matter more than a few pounds off.

decide: Insist on 16 GB RAM unless it is explicitly user-upgradable.
Ask for battery cycle count or health before buying.
Check the ports you need: many modern ultraportables dropped HDMI and USB-A.
Prefer ex-business chassis — they are built for daily handling and parts are easier to find.
posts.outro: Set a budget for a replacement battery in year two. Even a good refurb will likely need one before the course ends, and budgeting for it turns a risk into a plan.
